record_type_quote: In line with recent replication efforts in psychology (Klein et al., 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015), we combined data from three independent research groups, each conducting either exact (Group 1) or close conceptual (Groups 2 and 3) replications of Kidd and Castano (2013) to determine whether the original results could be replicated in a between-subjects design.

targets.title: Reading literary fiction improves theory of mind.
targets.evidence_quote: In line with recent replication efforts in psychology (Klein et al., 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015), we combined data from three independent research groups, each conducting either exact (Group 1) or close conceptual (Groups 2 and 3) replications of Kidd and Castano (2013) to determine whether the original results could be replicated in a between-subjects design.
targets.outcome_quote: We were unable to find significantly higher RMET scores after reading literary fiction compared to any of the other conditions. In short, we found no support for any short-term causal effects of reading literary fiction on theory of mind.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Overall discussion rejects the central short-term causal effect named in the title. The successful lifetime-exposure correlation is a control and does not change the failed central replication.

reasoning: Verified PDF title, DOI and all authors. Full nine-page advance article includes references. One target paper, across three research groups: Group 1 experiments 1, 3, 4 and 5 are reported, and Groups 2 and 3 each report unnumbered studies. replication_study_numbers contains Group 1 experiment numbers; Groups 2 and 3 are included in the aggregate verdict. Earlier replication attempts and correlational background papers are not targets. Original-data comparisons provide context for the new-data replication rather than a separate central reproduction attempt.
